Heavy rain is battering Mexico's northern Baja California peninsula after a post-tropical cyclone made landfall early this morning.
National Weather Service meteorologist Bob Oravec says the storm is expected to bring strong winds with flash flooding as it moves inland.
We have a potential for some widespread heavy rains from Southern California all the way northeastward through parts of Arizona, Southern Nevada, including Las Vegas and across much of Utah.
Along the Pacific coast of Mexico, Hurricane Simon is gaining strength with wind speeds of 155 miles per hour.
In the southeast, cleanup operations are underway after Hurricane Isaias made landfall in Florida on Friday.
Resident Andy Schultz says the damage for him was minimal.
We don't have power, don't have internet, but the power didn't go out until about nine. We do have water.
At least four people were killed when the storm hit.
Hundreds of thousands of customers remain without power in the region.
Many leaders of Native American tribal nations are raising concerns about the Trump administration's proposal for unprecedented changes to the next U.S. census.
NPR's Hansi Lo Wang reports.
Some post offices now have fewer daily pickups and a different way of processing mail to help the U.S. Postal Service stabilize its shaky finances.
Those changes have raised the risk of getting your mail-in ballot rejected if you mail it close to Election Day.
About a week before November 3rd, the Postal Service says it plans to speed up ballot deliveries.
Still, a USPS public service announcement says if you're voting by mail, do it early.
We recommend that you mail your completed ballot before Election Day and at least a week before the deadline by which your mail-in ballot must be received by your local election office.
Motors with mail-in ballots can also consider returning them at their local election office or at any available drop boxes.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
President Trump is facing pushback for the administration's move to sanction the International Criminal Court.
Dan Carpinschuck reports Canada has joined several European countries in supporting the international organization.
Canada signed a joint statement with Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and Britain, saying they disagree strongly with the sanctions and reaffirmed their continued support for the integrity of the international court.
They warned the sanctions would have a significant impact on the work of the court in trying to bring those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called the court fake, adding that Washington will cripple its ability to operate against the U.S.
The White House wants to dismantle the tribunal because of its investigations into the U.S. and its allies, namely Israel.
The sanctions were announced after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African jurist Navi Pillay on Friday.
For NPR News, I'm Dan Carpinschuck in Toronto.
This is NPR News.
Pope Leo says he'll undergo an operation in the coming days after doctors found a nodule in his lung.
The pontiff says it was detected at a very early stage and is well localized.
Doctors are recommending surgery, and the pope says he plans to follow their advice.
It's pumpkin spice season, and some shoppers are paying a lot more for their fall-themed products. NPR's Stephen Bissaha reports prices for pumpkin flavors are higher this year.
There's an almost 9 percent pumpkin spice premium, up a bit from last year.
Matt Schultz is chief consumer finance analyst at Lending Tree, which did the research.
He says some of the spooky season bump could be because pumpkins are slightly more expensive this year, but also...
Retailers understand how much people love pumpkin spice and how they might be willing to pay a little bit extra for it.
Now, this does vary by store.
If you take the time to look around at different places, you might be able to save yourself a little money.
Out of the six retailers it looked at, Lending Tree says Starbucks and Trader Joe's had the biggest fall flavor hikes.
Stephen Bissaha, NPR News.
Investigators have recovered to Renoir paintings stolen from a museum in southern France and arrested six people in connection with the theft.
The local mayor is praising investigators for finding the artworks and tracking down the suspects.
The thieves cut through a fence and climbed in through a window, taking four paintings in less than three minutes.
They abandoned two as they fled.
This is NPR News in Washington.
